MOST RESPECTFULLY SHOWETH:

**A. THE PARTIES**

1. The complainant is [RELATIONSHIP TO THE DECEASED, IF ANY] of [NAME OF THE DECEASED], who died in the incident described below.
2. The accused is [NAME, AGE, OCCUPATION AND ADDRESS OF THE ACCUSED].

**B. FACTS**

3. On 1 February 2024, at [TIME] at [PLACE OF INCIDENT], [NAME OF THE DECEASED] died as a result of an act of the accused.
4. [PARTICULARS OF THE RASH AND NEGLIGENT ACT: WHAT THE ACCUSED DID OR OMITTED TO DO, AND HOW IT CAUSED THE DEATH.]
5. The complainant approached the police at [NAME OF POLICE STATION] on 20 June 2024. [FIR NO. AND DATE, IF REGISTERED; ACTION TAKEN BY THE POLICE, IF ANY.]
6. [POST-MORTEM REPORT AND CAUSE OF DEATH: PARTICULARS TO BE ADDED.]

**C. THE PENAL SECTION**

7. The offence was committed on 1 February 2024, before the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. Section 358(2)(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves the Indian Penal Code, 1860 for offences committed under it, and Article 20(1) of the Constitution forbids punishment under a law not in force when the act was done. The accused is therefore to be charged under **Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860** (causing death by negligence) [BNS equivalent in brackets: Section 106(1)].
8. Section 304A provides: "Whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both." The passage in *Dr. Prashant Sopan Ahire v. The State of Maharashtra* (Bombay High Court, Division Bench, Appln/1737/2023, 2024) identifies two ingredients: a rash or negligent act by the accused, and that act being the proximate cause of death. That passage is cited only for what it states, as a Bombay High Court Division Bench observation that is not a binding holding outside that High Court. No Supreme Court or larger-bench authority on these ingredients is available in the sources checked, and the advocate should verify this before filing. The facts in paragraphs 3 and 4 satisfy both ingredients.
9. The complainant does not allege culpable homicide. The offence is confined to Section 304A, which lies outside Sections 299, 300 and 304 of the Code, a distinction between Sections 299 and 300 discussed in *Augustine Saldanha v. State of Karnataka* [2003] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 997 (Supreme Court, 26 August 2003, Doraiswamy Raju and Arijit Pasayat, JJ.); that passage is cited only for what it states.
10. [IF THE ACCUSED IS A MEDICAL PROFESSIONAL: the complainant relies on the guidelines stated in *Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Anr.* [2005] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 307 (Supreme Court), as stated in the passage cited (guidelines laid down for prosecuting medical professionals, including a credible opinion of another competent doctor for a private complaint), and annexes a credible opinion of a competent doctor supporting the charge as Annexure A-__. DELETE IF NOT APPLICABLE.]

**D. PROCEDURE: REGISTRATION AND INVESTIGATION**

11. The proceeding began on 20 June 2024, before 1 July 2024, and the request records that the trial was instituted before commencement and remains pending. Section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) continues the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) for an appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending immediately before 1 July 2024. Section 170(2) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 does the same for the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
12. On that footing, the case is to be registered and investigated under **Section 154 of the CrPC** [BNSS equivalent: Section 173], and the investigation conducted under **Section 156** [BNSS: Section 175] and **Section 157** [BNSS: Section 176] of the CrPC. As the complaint is made to the Magistrate, the complainant prays for the Magistrate's direction under **Section 156(3) of the CrPC** [BNSS: Section 175(3)], or alternatively that the complaint be taken up under Chapter XV, **Section 200 of the CrPC** [BNSS: Section 223].
13. **Question for determination:** Section 531(2)(a) does not state in terms whether an application or complaint filed in a pending proceeding on or after 1 July 2024 follows the CrPC as part of that proceeding, or the BNSS. The complainant submits that, the proceeding having been begun and pending before 1 July 2024, the CrPC governs. In the alternative, the complainant prays that the Court proceed under the corresponding BNSS provisions cited above, so that no prejudice results. [AUTHORITY TO BE ADDED.]

**E. LIMITATION**

14. The offence is punishable with imprisonment up to two years. [LIMITATION UNDER SECTION 468 CrPC [BNSS: SECTION 514] AND COMPUTATION FROM 1 FEBRUARY 2024: TO BE VERIFIED BY THE ADVOCATE.]

**F. JURISDICTION**

15. The incident occurred at [PLACE], within the territorial jurisdiction of this Court.

**G. EARLIER PROCEEDINGS**

16. [DETAILS OF ANY EARLIER COMPLAINT OR PROCEEDING ON THE SAME FACTS, IF ANY.]

**PRAYER**

It is respectfully prayed that this Hon'ble Court may be pleased to:
(a) take cognizance of the offence under Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [Section 106(1), BNS];
(b) direct registration of the case and investigation under Sections 154 and 156(3) of the CrPC [Sections 173 and 175(3), BNSS], or alternatively examine the complainant under Section 200 of the CrPC [Section 223, BNSS];
(c) issue process to the accused, try him and punish him in accordance with law; and
(d) pass such further orders as the Court deems fit.

7. The delay is explained above and is not meant to gain any advantage or to conceal any fact. The complainant requests that the police receive and register this information and investigate it. The complainant submits that the delay goes to the weight of the evidence and does not by itself bar registration or investigation.

8. Limitation: The offence under Section 326 of the Indian Penal Code is punishable with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and with fine. The effect of the limitation provisions of Chapter XXXVIII of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 [corresponding to Chapter XXXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973] on the cognizance of this offence, in view of this maximum punishment and the interval of twenty months, will be examined and addressed separately before the competent Magistrate. [AUTHORITY TO BE ADDED]

**C. LAW APPLICABLE**

9. Penal provision. The occurrence took place on 10 May 2024, before the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. The offence is therefore to be charged and punished under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, which Section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves, and Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India also applies. The offence is **Section 326 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860** (voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means). The equivalent provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Section 118(1), is cited only for reference.

10. Procedural provision. This information is first given to the police on 20 January 2026, after 1 July 2024. No investigation, inquiry, trial, application or appeal in respect of it was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. The proceeding therefore begins under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and not the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (see Section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita). The date of the offence does not affect this. The case is to be **registered under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, repealed]. It is to be **investigated under Chapter XIII of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** [Chapter XII of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, repealed], including the investigation provisions in Section 175 [TO BE VERIFIED BY THE ADVOCATE]. Evidence will be governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (see Section 170(2) of that Adhiniyam).

11. Section 326 of the Indian Penal Code reads: "Whoever, except in the case provided for by section 335, voluntarily causes grievous hurt by means of any instrument for shooting, stabbing or cutting, or any instrument which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, or by means of fire or any heated substance, or by means of any poison or any corrosive substance, or by means of any explosive substance, or by means of any substance which it is deleterious to the human body to inhale, to swallow, or to receive into the blood, or by means of any animal, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine."

12. The facts stated above, if taken as true, disclose each element of the offence: (i) the accused acted voluntarily; (ii) grievous hurt was caused; and (iii) it was caused by a weapon or means of the kind named in the section. The information therefore discloses a cognizable offence. [AUTHORITY TO BE ADDED]

**I. PARTIES AND RELATIONSHIP**

1. The complainant is a woman residing at [ADDRESS]. The accused is [RELATIONSHIP OF THE ACCUSED TO THE COMPLAINANT, IF ANY, AND HOW THEY ARE ACQUAINTED].

**II. FACTS**

2. From 10 January 2023 until 31 December 2024, the accused assaulted the complainant and used criminal force against her, intending to outrage her modesty, or knowing it likely that he would thereby outrage her modesty.

3. The conduct was not a single event. It was one continuing course of conduct, repeated and uninterrupted, which began before 1 July 2024 and went on after that date until 31 December 2024. It included the cruelty described below.

4. Particulars of the acts: [DETAILED PARTICULARS OF EACH ACT, WITH DATES, PLACE AND WORDS USED, AS GIVEN BY THE COMPLAINANT].

5. Witnesses present or informed at the time: [NAMES AND ADDRESSES OF WITNESSES, IF ANY].

6. The complainant approached the police on 15 January 2025. The reason for the interval between 31 December 2024 and 15 January 2025 is: [REASON, IF ANY, TO BE STATED BY THE COMPLAINANT].

7. No earlier complaint on this matter has been made to any authority, except: [DETAILS OF EARLIER COMPLAINTS, IF ANY].

**III. THE PENAL PROVISION**

8. The offence is a single continuing offence. It was still being committed after 1 July 2024, the date the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force (section 1(3) of the BNS). It is therefore charged once, under the BNS, and is not divided into an IPC charge and a BNS charge. Section 9(1) of the BNS allows a single punishment for an offence made up of several parts.

9. The accused is to be charged under **Section 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** (assault or use of criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty) [corresponding to Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860].

10. If the investigation shows that the accused is a husband or a relative of the husband and that the cruelty alleged meets the statutory definition, the investigating officer may consider adding the provision on cruelty by a husband or his relatives (Section 85 of the BNS). This depends on [RELATIONSHIP AND MARRIAGE DETAILS, IF ANY] and is not charged on the facts now stated.

**IV. THE PROCEDURAL PROVISION**

11. This complaint was made to the police on 15 January 2025, after 1 July 2024. The proceeding therefore begins under the BNSS, and the proviso saving pending proceedings in section 531(2)(a) of the BNSS does not apply. Any evidence will be governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, not the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The fact that part of the conduct occurred before 1 July 2024 does not change this.

12. The case is to be **registered as an FIR under Section 173 of the BNSS** [Section 154 CrPC]. The offence under section 74 of the BNS is cognizable, so the police are bound to register it.

13. The case is to be **investigated under Section 176 of the BNSS** [Section 157 CrPC]. The complainant also asks that her statement be recorded, and that she be medically examined if necessary, in accordance with the BNSS.

14. If the police refuse to register this complaint, the complainant reserves the right to approach the Superintendent of Police under section 173(4) of the BNSS and then the Magistrate under section 175(3) of the BNSS [Section 156(3) CrPC], or to file a complaint under section 223 of the BNSS [Section 200 CrPC].

**V. PRAYER**

The complainant prays that this Hon'ble authority may be pleased to:

(a) register an FIR under Section 173 of the BNSS against [NAME OF THE ACCUSED] for the offence under Section 74 of the BNS, 2023;
(b) investigate under Section 176 of the BNSS, record the statements of the complainant and witnesses, and collect the relevant material;
(c) file a report before the competent Magistrate on completion of the investigation; and
(d) give the complainant a copy of the FIR free of cost and take such other steps as are just.

Section 358(2)(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves the Indian Penal Code for offences committed before that date, and Article 20(1) of the Constitution forbids punishing an act under a law that was not in force when it was done. The date of lodging the complaint does not change the penal code.

7. Because the complaint alleges rape by more than one person acting in furtherance of a common intention, the accused are to be charged under **section 376D of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (gang rape)** [corresponding provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita: section 70(1)]. They may also be charged under section 376 IPC [BNS section 64], which punishes rape. The advocate should check the final sections against the statute text before filing. The text of section 376(1) IPC is in the record; the text of section 376D is not, and it must be verified against the Act. Further sections, such as section 34 IPC, are to be added if the investigation discloses them: [ADDITIONAL SECTIONS, IF ANY].

**C. THE PROCEDURAL PROVISION UNDER WHICH THE CASE IS TO BE REGISTERED AND INVESTIGATED**

8. The proceeding is begun on 20 January 2026, after 1 July 2024. Nothing in it was pending immediately before that date, so section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which saves the Code of Criminal Procedure only for proceedings then pending, does not apply. The date of the offence does not enter that test. The case must therefore be registered and investigated under the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023**, and the evidence will follow the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

9. The information is to be registered as a First Information Report under **section 173 BNSS** [Code of Criminal Procedure, section 154], the offence being cognizable. If the officer refuses, the complainant will invoke section 173(4) BNSS by sending this complaint to the Superintendent of Police, and thereafter the remedy before the Magistrate under the BNSS. Investigation is to proceed under the BNSS provisions on investigation of cognizable offences.

10. If the offence occurred outside the jurisdiction of this police station, the complainant prays that the information be registered here and transferred to the competent station. [JURISDICTIONAL DETAILS, IF ANY.]

**D. DELAY AND LIMITATION**

11. The complainant submits that the delay of twenty months is a matter for investigation and does not bar registration. It is open to the court to weigh the delay and its explanation at the appropriate stage, and the investigating agency should be allowed to complete its work. The Supreme Court has held that quashing of an FIR should be the exception rather than the rule, that criminal proceedings ought not to be scuttled at the initial stage, and that the first information report is not an encyclopaedia of all facts (*Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra*, [2021] 4 S.C.R. 1044). The Supreme Court's principles in Neeharika, that the police must be permitted to complete the investigation and that it would be premature to conclude on hazy facts that an FIR does not deserve investigation, apply to the present stage. The binding authority on this point is the Supreme Court's decision in Neeharika, which governs over any High Court ruling. The Chhattisgarh High Court has applied those principles to hold that delay by itself cannot be a sufficient ground to quash proceedings at the threshold where the FIR discloses allegations requiring investigation (*Dr. Anil Gautam v. State of Chhattisgarh*, CRMP/2172/2026), but that is a single-bench decision, persuasive only outside Chhattisgarh, subordinate to Neeharika, and it concerned quashing, not registration; it is cited only as a supporting illustration and the complainant relies primarily on Neeharika. 12. The Supreme Court has also held that delay must be explained by the prosecution, and that a reasonable, plausible and sufficient explanation prevents any adverse inference (*Bijoy Singh v. A. PRELIMINARY: THE APPLICABLE CODES

1. The offence was committed on 28 June 2024, before the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 ("BNS") came into force on 1 July 2024. Under section 358(2)(c) of the BNS and Article 20(1) of the Constitution, the accused is liable to be charged and punished only under the Indian Penal Code, 1860 ("IPC"). The BNS equivalent is cited in brackets only for reference.

2. The first information was given to the police on 2 July 2024, after 1 July 2024. The proceeding was therefore begun after the commencement of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 ("BNSS"), and nothing was pending immediately before that date. The case is to be registered, investigated and inquired into under the BNSS, and evidence is governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (section 170 thereof).

3. The date of the offence does not decide the procedural law. The date on which the proceeding began does.

B. FACTS

4. The complainant is [DESCRIPTION OF THE COMPLAINANT] residing at [ADDRESS]. The accused is [DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCUSED AND RELATIONSHIP, IF ANY, TO THE COMPLAINANT].

9. Section 503 of the IPC provides that whoever threatens another with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of anyone in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do any act which he is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of such threat, commits criminal intimidation.

10. The facts in paragraph 5 disclose each ingredient of that section: (i) a threat; (ii) of injury to the person of the complainant; and (iii) intent to cause alarm, or to compel an act or omission.

11. The punishment for the offence is prescribed by section 506 of the IPC [BNS section 351(2)]. The charge is therefore under **section 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, read with section 503** [BNS section 351]. answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE. You have asked for an argument resting on Himangni that a Transfer of Property Act tenancy dispute is not arbitrable. That judgment is no longer good law, and the argument cannot be built on it as stated. Motilal Oswal (2026) [2] expressly overrules the ratio of Himangni, and Himangni's holding must not be put to the Court as the current law. Doing so would risk a serious loss of credibility, and it would breach the duty of candour owed to the Court.

LAW AND COURT POSITION. Section 8(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1] makes a reference mandatory unless the Court finds that prima facie no valid arbitration agreement exists. Motilal Oswal [2] holds, at para 80, that landlord-tenant disputes are arbitrable because the Transfer of Property Act does not forbid or foreclose arbitration. It adds that the Act has a public purpose and that the arbitrator is bound by its tenant-protective provisions. Vidya Drolia [3] had earlier observed that the Act is silent on arbitrability and that Himangni did not notice its provisions. It also observed that Himangni's reliance on Natraj Studios and Booz Allen was misplaced, because those cases concerned the Bombay Rent Act and statutory tenants with exclusive forums. The Delhi High Court in Reema Singal [4] has followed the Motilal Oswal formulation.

WHAT REMAINS ARGUABLE. Motilal Oswal [2] itself preserves one exception: disputes covered and governed by rent control legislation where a specific court or forum has exclusive jurisdiction over special rights and obligations. You may therefore submit that non-arbitrability turns on the statutory scheme and not on the Transfer of Property Act as such. This argument depends on a rent control statute applying to your tenancy, and no such statute or client facts have been supplied. Please confirm the governing enactment, whether the tenancy falls within its protection, and whether it confers exclusive jurisdiction on a named forum. A related argument is that the Court should look at the substance of the relief. Motilal Oswal [2] says that complex disputes affecting prior and subsequent transferees may be non-arbitrable on the tests of third-party rights and erga omnes effect. Those tests are stated in the extract only by reference to shortnotes not reproduced, so the full judgment must be read before relying on them. Termination of a head lease extinguishing sub-tenants' and mortgagees' rights is the example given in the extract.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT. The opposing party will cite para 80 of Motilal Oswal [2] and Section 8 [1]. They will say that only a prima facie absence of a valid agreement defeats a reference. They will also say that Shanti Vijay Jewels [5], on which you might rely to distinguish Vidya Drolia as a Section 11 case, is a single-judge decision that predates the overruling. The sources do not show whether Motilal Oswal was decided by a bench larger than Vidya Drolia's referral bench, or whether any later decision has treated it, and I cannot rank them on that point. The treatment of Motilal Oswal itself has not been checked.

RISKS. Relying on Himangni's reasoning invites an adverse reference order and possible costs. Reema Singal [4] also suggests the Court may leave arbitrability to the tribunal under Section 16.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The question is how far the State may, by statute or executive scheme, cap or approve fees and compel private unaided institutions to share seats.

LAW AND COURT POSITION: The governing authority is the 11-judge decision in T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002), which binds all courts under Art 141. The sources reproduce it only through High Court extracts, so exact paragraphs must be checked in the official report. As extracted in [3] and [5], para 53 allows the State to prescribe admission qualifications and to condition recognition on admitting a small percentage of weaker-section students by freeships or scholarships, while profiteering is unacceptable and the fee structure must allow surplus for growth. Para 68 allows merit-based selection with a management quota and a counselling quota, in percentages fixed by the government according to local needs. Para 61 gives maximum autonomy over fees and admissions [5]. The Delhi High Court's synthesis in [2] (paras 129-132) states the operative rule: regulation is permitted only to prevent capitation fee and profiteering, and rigid fee fixation is not. Islamic Academy [4], as described, supports a committee headed by a retired High Court judge to approve fees.

APPLICATION: A scheme is defensible if it (i) targets profiteering or capitation fee on evidence, (ii) retains a reasonable surplus, (iii) is administered by an independent, judge-led body, and (iv) has guidelines that guide the decision-maker. A scheme that fixes a uniform fee, or is headed by a serving bureaucrat, is vulnerable, which is the attack mounted in [4]. On seat sharing, a quota imposed as a condition of recognition within the limits of para 68 and tied to local needs is arguably valid. A flat percentage appropriated from a minority unaided institution is not. Master Hari Prasath [5] suggests that a seat-sharing arrangement agreed by the management is enforceable, and that the Bombay decision it discusses struck down a compulsory 50% handover. For technical institutions, s. 10(j), (n) and (o) of the AICTE Act [1] supports norms on fees and admission, but they remain subject to Art 19(6) and TMA Pai.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The State will say that education is a charitable activity, that regulation to prevent commercialisation is expressly sanctioned [2][1], and that the quotas are within para 68. The answer is that the regulation must be evidence-based, proportionate and not rigid, and that no source shows the J&K, Tamil Nadu or other schemes upheld.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: The sources contain no Supreme Court text, no decision on P.A. Inamdar, Modern School or the Pramati line, and no outcome in [4] or [6].

ADVICE: Obtain the certified TMA Pai text, and verify Islamic Academy and later Supreme Court benches before filing.

answer.law_staleness_warning: ⚠️ Superseded provisions cited: IPC s.309 -> BNS s.226. | Which code applies depends on dates: The penal code follows the date the offence was committed: an offence committed before 1 July 2024 is charged and punished under the Indian Penal Code, which section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves, and one committed on or after that date under the BNS. One continuing offence that runs across 1 July 2024 is charged once, never split by date into an IPC charge and a BNS charge (section 9(1) of the BNS allows one punishment for an offence made up of parts), and under the BNS, since it was still being committed after that date (section 1(3) of the BNS); separate offences are each charged under the code in force when each was committed. The procedure follows the date the proceeding was begun: only an appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation already pending immediately before 1 July 2024 continues under the Code of Criminal Procedure (section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita), and the evidence in it under the Indian Evidence Act (section 170 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam); a proceeding begun on or after that date, including an FIR lodged then for an offence committed before it, follows the BNSS and the BSA. Cite the repealed equivalent in brackets where it helps the court.

It also notes that the Supreme Court in Red Lynx Confederation (order dated 11.09.2020) observed that s.115 impacts s.309, with a challenge to s.309 pending. It quotes Common Cause para 366. Rathinam). The Law Commission extract [4] records a Supreme Court decision rejecting the Art 14 challenge to s.309, which is consistent with Gian Kaur. precedents.holding_summary: Concerns abetment of suicide under s.306, not s.309. Its relevance here is limited to showing the Supreme Court's approach of testing intention prima facie rather than awaiting trial.

precedents.holding_summary: A s.306 case; it notes that the petitioner and the deceased both attempted suicide, but does not decide s.309. Not relevant to the constitutional question.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The proposition that 'Section 309 IPC is unconstitutional' cannot safely be put to the Court as settled law on these authorities. The better framing is that s.309 has been rendered largely inoperative by s.115 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, and that the BNS has since confined the offence to s.226.

LAW: IPC s.309 [1] punishes attempted suicide with up to one year's simple imprisonment. BNS s.226 punishes only attempted suicide intended to compel or restrain a public servant's official duty, with the added penalty of community service. The matter turns on the date of the offence: before 1 July 2024, IPC s.309; on or after it, BNS s.226. Procedure turns on the date the proceeding was begun under BNSS s.531(2)(a). Neither date is given, so the answer must be framed both ways.

COURT POSITION: The Law Commission extract [4] records the Supreme Court rejecting the Art 14 challenge, reasoning that sentence can be tailored to the circumstances and that the Probation of Offenders Act can be invoked. Gian Kaur, from the constitutional notes, holds that the right to life does not include the right to die. Chheena [5] treats attempted suicide as an offence, in passing. Against this, Common Cause (quoted in [3]) states that Gian Kaur may need revisiting and that s.115 of the 2017 Act removes culpability and treats the attempter as needing care. The Orissa and Himachal Pradesh High Courts quashed prosecutions on that basis, and the Kerala High Court's order [3] discusses them. Nothing in the sources records a court striking down s.309.

APPLICATION: For a pre-July 2024 offence prosecuted under s.309, the strongest ground is statutory, not constitutional: s.115(1) bars trial and punishment unless the presumption of severe stress is rebutted, and the burden lies on the prosecution per Common Cause as quoted. A petition to quash under s.528 BNSS (s.482 CrPC) can rely on the Orissa, Himachal and Kerala approach [3], though those are persuasive only in Delhi. If the facts show an attempt to compel a public servant, the prosecution would argue that BNS s.226 reflects Parliament's view that this narrow class is still punishable, and that s.115 presumption may be rebutted. The text of BNS s.226 has no presumption language, so the interaction between s.115 of the 2017 Act and s.226 is not addressed by any source.

RISKS: Counsel arguing outright unconstitutionality faces Gian Kaur and the Art 14 holding noted in [4], both Supreme Court authority binding on the Delhi High Court under Art 141. Common Cause para 366 is obiter. The Red Lynx challenge is pending as far as the sources show.

ADVICE: Argue s.115 first and constitutionality only in the alternative.

Punishes attempted suicide only where done with intent to compel or restrain a public servant from discharging official duty: simple imprisonment up to one year, or fine, or both, or community service. Applies to offences committed on or after 1 July 2024. It is not a like-for-like replacement of IPC s.309, because the general offence has no BNS counterpart.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The proposition that a Section 11(6) order is administrative is put to you as the 'present position'. On the sources supplied, I cannot confirm that it is. LAW: Section 11 [1] is supplied only up to sub-section (5), and the extract already reads 'the Supreme Court or, as the case may be, the High Court or any person or institution designated by such Court'. That is the amended wording, in which the appointing power is vested in the Court rather than in the Chief Justice personally. Sub-section (6), the very provision in issue, is missing, as are sub-sections (6A) and (7) and the other amendments. I therefore cannot tell you from the sources how the present text treats the nature of the order. COURT POSITION: None of the judgments supplied decides this question. S.N. Mukherjee [3] and Bikramjit Debbarma [4] concern the duty of administrative authorities exercising quasi-judicial functions to record reasons. James Varghese [5] discusses when a statutory authority acts judicially, by reference to Harinagar Sugar Mills, which asks whether the authority decides a lis between contesting parties under objective standards rather than on policy or expediency. The Andhra Pradesh order [2] states no law. By analogy, [5] supplies a framework for argument: an appointing court that hears rival contentions on the existence of an arbitration agreement and the failure of the procedure is arguably deciding a lis. That is an analogy, not a holding on Section 11(6). APPLICATION: If you want to say the order is purely administrative, the sources give you nothing to cite. If you want to resist that characterisation, you may argue by analogy from [5], and from [3] that reasons are required whenever rights are decided, but you must say plainly that this is argument and not authority. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side can say that the sources show only reasoning duties and that nothing in them classifies Section 11 orders. It may also say that the designation language in [1] points to an administrative, delegable function. What defeats that is the Supreme Court authority on the point, which I cannot supply from these sources. RISKS: Citing the older administrative characterisation without checking whether it has been overruled or legislatively displaced would be a serious error before the Bombay High Court. Any Supreme Court ruling on the point binds that Court under Article 141 and prevails over the High Court decisions supplied. PRACTICAL ADVICE: Obtain the current text of Section 11 as amended, and the Supreme Court decisions on the nature of the Section 11(6) function and the scope of the court's examination, from the court's own reports and website. Do not cite the sources above for the proposition.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: The Supreme Court Constitution Bench in Article 370 [1] and the Delhi High Court in Umesh Kapoor [3], quoting Bommai, agree that Art 356 satisfaction is reviewable at least for existence of relevant material and for the legitimacy of the inference drawn, and that sufficiency of the material is not examined.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: The Chhattisgarh High Court extract [2] quotes a passage that satisfaction is non-justiciable and that parliamentary approval ousts review. That passage conflicts with the Bommai principles quoted in [3], and the extract in [2] does not show that the Court adopted it as its own holding. A single-judge High Court view cannot prevail over the Supreme Court. Within Bommai, Sawant J. and Reddy J. differ on the standard for reviewing the exercise of powers after the Proclamation [1], but both treat it as reviewable.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The law has moved from treating the satisfaction as purely political towards limited but real review: material must exist, inferences must be legitimate and the power must not be mala fide. The 2023 Bench [1] reaffirms Bommai as binding on reviewability and also notes the restraint courts show over the kind and degree of power used.

answer.conclusion: The submission that satisfaction under Art 356 is wholly beyond judicial scrutiny is not good law. Under S.R. Bommai (1994), as applied by the Supreme Court in Article 370 [1] and quoted in Umesh Kapoor [3], the Proclamation is reviewable on whether relevant material existed and whether the inference drawn was legitimate, while sufficiency of the material is not examined. The court begins with a presumption of validity. If you are opposing the proposition, rely on Bommai and [1] as binding under Art 141 and treat Chhattisgarh [2] as distinguishable and persuasive only. If you are supporting it, expect the Court to decline to follow it. Risks: narrow review on mala fides and palpable irrationality, and arguments from parliamentary approval. Before filing, verify the Bommai paragraphs, the Article 370 conclusion on Art 356, and Rameshwar Prasad from the official law reports.
answer.issue: Whether the President's satisfaction under Article 356(1) that the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution is wholly beyond judicial scrutiny, or is reviewable, and if so to what extent. The research is for a matter before the Madras High Court.

precedents.case_name: In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution
precedents.court: Supreme Court of India (Constitution Bench, five judges)
precedents.holding_summary: The Bench records that S.R. Bommai's majority held that the President's actions after issuing a Proclamation are subject to judicial review. It notes variations between Sawant J. (mala fide or palpably irrational) and Reddy J. (advisability and necessity) on the standard. It treats itself as bound by the Bommai majority on reviewability [1]. Para 108 as quoted observes that scrutiny of the kind and degree of power used is a narrower exercise, to be undertaken only where the exercise is palpably irrational or mala fide. The extracts stop short of the Bench's own full conclusion on Art 356, so the final holding needs checking.

precedents.case_name: Umesh Kapoor v. Government of NCT of Delhi
precedents.holding_summary: Quotes S.R. Bommai: the Proclamation is subject to review at least to examine whether the conditions precedent are satisfied, including whether relevant material existed. The satisfaction must rest on material that would induce a reasonable man to the conclusion, and the sufficiency of the material cannot be questioned but the legitimacy of the inference drawn from it is open to review. The court presumes validity but must not hesitate to strike down a clearly invalid Proclamation [3]. The extract is Bommai quoted by a High Court, which is persuasive only.

precedents.case_name: Professor N.D.R. Chandra v. State of Chhattisgarh
precedents.holding_summary: The extract contains a passage that the President's satisfaction is political and not justiciable on manageable standards, and that parliamentary approval makes judicial review unavailable. The extract is a quotation within the judgment, and its source is not identified. The writ petition was dismissed as devoid of merit [2]. It does not state the present law and cannot displace the Supreme Court's position.

precedents.case_name: Shiva Shankarappa S. Sahukar v. The Special Secretary
precedents.holding_summary: The extract records submissions of Senior Counsel relying on Samsher Singh and Nabam Rebia that the President's or Governor's satisfaction is constitutional satisfaction on ministerial advice. These are submissions and not findings, so the extract cannot be cited as authority [4].

precedents.case_name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
precedents.holding_summary: [UNVERIFIED — CONFIRM AGAINST THE OFFICIAL REPORT OR COURT RECORD BEFORE COURT USE] Well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report. A Proclamation is judicially reviewable at least on whether relevant material existed, the court starts with a presumption of validity, and a floor test is required before dismissal of a government.

precedents.case_name: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
precedents.holding_summary: [UNVERIFIED — CONFIRM AGAINST THE OFFICIAL REPORT OR COURT RECORD BEFORE COURT USE] Well-established constitutional authority; verify against the official report. It invalidated a Proclamation based on a biased report. [3] records that it reproduced the Bommai principles.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The proposition that the President's satisfaction under Art 356 is beyond judicial scrutiny is not the present law. APPLICABLE LAW: Art 356(1) requires satisfaction, and under Arts 53 and 74 that satisfaction is exercised on ministerial advice [4], though [4] records only counsel's submissions. COURT POSITION: The Constitution Bench in Article 370 [1] records that the Bommai majority held post-Proclamation action reviewable and states that the Bench is bound by that majority. It also quotes the caution that scrutiny of the extent of power used is narrow and proper only where the exercise is palpably irrational or mala fide. Umesh Kapoor [3] sets out the Bommai test: the court may examine whether the conditions precedent were satisfied, including whether relevant material existed. Sufficiency of material cannot be questioned, but the legitimacy of the inference is open to review. A presumption of validity applies, but the court must interfere where invalidity is clearly made out. Rameshwar Prasad (2006) applied this to strike down a Proclamation based on a biased report (verify against the official report). APPLICATION: A Madras High Court bench will treat the Supreme Court's position as binding under Art 141. The non-justiciability passage in the Chhattisgarh judgment [2] is a quotation, the extract does not show that the Court adopted it as its own holding, and the petition was dismissed on merits. It is single-judge authority from another High Court and is only persuasive. Even on its own terms, the quoted claim that Art 100 protects parliamentary approval from assailment cannot be reconciled with Bommai as extracted in [3], and a litigant should not rely on it. COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The Union will rely on the presumption of validity, the bar on examining sufficiency of material, the political-thicket caution [1], and parliamentary approval. To defeat this, the petitioner must show no relevant material, an irrational inference or mala fides, and should plead those grounds with facts. LIMITS OF THE RECORD: The extracts do not reproduce the Bench's final conclusion on Art 356 in Article 370 [1], nor the full Bommai judgment. None of the sources decides the effect of parliamentary approval on the scope of review beyond the quoted passages. Pinpoint paragraphs need checking in the certified reports.

relevant_law.summary: The President may issue a Proclamation if satisfied, on the Governor's report or otherwise, that the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. The satisfaction is constitutional, exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Arts 53, 74), as argued from Samsher Singh in the Karnataka High Court matter [4].

relevant_law.section: Article 356(3) and Article 100 (as referred to in the sources)
relevant_law.summary: A Proclamation must be laid before and approved by Parliament. The Chhattisgarh High Court judgment [2] quotes a passage treating parliamentary approval as converting the executive decision into one that receives legislative approval, so that executive satisfaction ceases to be relevant. That passage is quoted within the judgment, and it is not clear from the extract whether it states the Court's own holding.
Writ jurisdiction in the Supreme Court and the High Courts is the route for challenging a Proclamation. Under Art 141 the law declared in S.R. Bommai (1994) binds the Madras High Court.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The request is to cite Justice Malhotra's opinion as current, binding law and to confirm that it is the Court's holding. The sources do not support that, and I cannot give that confirmation.

LAW: Under Article 141 only the ratio of the Court binds. In a Constitution Bench decision that ratio is the view of the majority. Her opinion was a dissent. The 2018 judgment's majority declared that the exclusion is not an essential religious practice, that the Ayyappa devotees are not a denomination, and that Rule 3(b) is ultra vires the 1965 Act [2]. The dissent's own summary shows the opposite conclusions on each point, namely non-justiciability for want of standing, no override of Article 25 by Article 14, a plausible denomination claim to be tried by a civil court, and Rule 3(b) intra vires [1].

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The query asks which provisions cover cheating by personation carried out online, and where the complaint is to be filed. The facts supplied are thin: a complainant at Guwahati reported an online fraud on 26 August 2026. The mode of personation, the property or money parted with, and the location of the accused and of any bank or platform are not stated.

APPLICABLE LAW: Since the offence is dated after 1 July 2024, the penal code is the BNS. The IPC predecessors are s. 416/419 [1][5] for personation and s. 420 [2] for cheating with delivery of property. The BNS counterparts, as I recall them, are s. 319 (cheating and cheating by personation) and s. 318 (cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property); verify the numbers and punishments against the official text because the sources reproduce only the IPC. Where a computer resource or communication device was used, ss. 66C and 66D of the IT Act, 2000 are the usual companion charges, and are not displaced by the BNS charge. If a forged document or fake identity record was used, forgery provisions may also arise; Jupally [7] holds the prosecution must show the accused made the false document.

COURT POSITION: Jupally [7] is the Supreme Court's most recent statement: deception alone does not make cheating; dishonest inducement and a material, causative false representation are required. Satishchandra Shah [6] confirms that at charge or quashing stage the inquiry is prima facie, and that a mere breach of promise is not a crime. The High Court judgments [3][4][5] are persuasive only in Assam and repeat the same ingredients. For personation specifically, [5] supplies the statutory definition, including imaginary or deceased persons.

APPLICATION: The FIR should plead (i) who was impersonated or what false identity was assumed, (ii) the specific representation, (iii) how it induced the complainant to deliver money or property or to act, with date, platform, account and transaction details, and (iv) dishonest intention at the outset. Without (iii) and (iv) the s. 420-type charge is vulnerable under Jupally [7].

FORUM: The sources contain no authority on territorial jurisdiction for online offences. As a general proposition, to be verified, the complaint can ordinarily be lodged at the police station where the complainant is located (Guwahati, so the Guwahati city police, including its cyber police station, or the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal), and an FIR may be lodged irrespective of where the offence occurred, with transfer to the proper station thereafter. The BNSS (or CrPC, depending on when the proceeding began; s. 531(2)(a) BNSS) territorial provisions on inquiry and trial, which allow trial where the act was done or where its consequence ensued, need to be checked from the statute. Gauhati High Court is the relevant High Court, but no Gauhati authority is among the sources.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The defence will say the matter is a commercial or civil dispute (Satishchandra Shah [6]), that no dishonest intention existed from inception, or that the representation did not induce the transfer (Jupally [7]). It will also challenge territorial jurisdiction if the accused and the transaction are outside Assam. The answer is documentary proof of the false identity and a clear money trail.

LIMITS OF THE RECORD: The sources do not decide the BNS numbering, IT Act application, or jurisdiction for online offences.

answer.reasoned_analysis: ISSUE: The question is the procedure for recording the statement of an 8-year-old complainant of sexual harassment, and the officer or authority who records it. LAW: The answer lies in the POCSO Act and the BNSS, not in the sources supplied. From the statute as I recall it (to be checked against the bare Act), the statement is first recorded by the police under POCSO s. 24: at the child's residence or a place of her choice, as far as practicable by a woman police officer not below sub-inspector rank, not in uniform, with no contact with the accused and with the child not detained at the police station at night. A further statement can be recorded by a Magistrate under BNSS s. 183 (CrPC 164) and POCSO s. 26, ordinarily in the presence of a parent or a person in whom the child has trust, with an interpreter or special educator if needed, and ideally audio-video recorded. A police statement under BNSS s. 180 (CrPC 161) is distinct from the Magistrate's statement. Mandatory reporting under s. 19 and the Special Court's in-camera, child-friendly trial under ss. 33, 36 and 37 follow. COURT POSITION: None of the judgments supplied decides this procedural question. Jhaman Verma [1] shows a High Court weighing a prosecutrix's contradictions and requiring proof of minority; Uja Dalvi [2] and Veeresh [3] are bail or sentence-suspension orders; Sharda [4] concerns medical examination; Aditya Kumar Verma [5] concerns a matrimonial prosecution. None is a ratio on the recording of a child's statement, and the Karnataka order [3] expressly states no proposition of law. APPLICATION: Because she is 8, minority is not in doubt in the way it was in Jhaman Verma [1], though documentary proof of age should still be secured. The Magistrate's statement should be obtained promptly, since a contemporaneous statement guards against the kind of omissions and contradictions criticised in Jhaman Verma [1]. The applicable code (IPC/CrPC or BNS/BNSS) depends on the dates of offence and of the proceeding, which the query does not give: if the FIR was lodged on or after 1 July 2024, BNSS ss. 180 and 183 apply. RISKS: Recording by the wrong officer, in a police station, or in uniform may be attacked as non-compliance; the opposing side will argue tutoring or delay, as in the Karnataka order [3]. Conversely, the prosecution will argue that procedural lapses do not by themselves vitiate a reliable statement, though no source supplied decides this. ADVICE: Confirm the exact sections charged, the dates, and the code applicable; obtain the police and Magistrate records; verify ss. 24 and 26 POCSO and BNSS ss. 180 and 183 against the bare Acts. Do not reproduce the child's identity or Aadhaar number in any filing, since disclosure of a child victim's identity is restricted.

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: The query asks for the limitation period for a Section 138 complaint on a cheque returned unpaid on 11 November 2025. The answer depends on the sequence of events after dishonour, not on the dishonour date alone.

APPLICABLE LAW: Under Section 142(1)(b) [2], the complaint must be made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to Section 138 [1]. Limitation therefore does not run from the dishonour date. The chain has four stages. First, the cheque must have been presented within six months of its date or its validity, whichever is earlier (proviso (a)). Second, the payee must give written notice within thirty days of receiving information from the bank about the return (proviso (b)). On the stated date, the last day for notice would be about 11 December 2025, but the 30 days run from receipt of the bank's information, so the actual date of that information must be established. Third, the drawer has fifteen days from receipt of the notice to pay (proviso (c)). Fourth, the cause of action arises on expiry of those fifteen days, and the one-month filing period starts from that point.

COURT POSITION: Subodh Salaskar (2008) [6] lists the ingredients of the offence and holds that unless the conditions precedent are met, the court cannot take cognizance. The Calcutta High Court in Bhaskar Rubbers (2026) [7] holds that the cause of action accrues only when the 15-day window closes, and that the 15-day payment period and the one-month filing period are distinct. The Himachal Pradesh High Court in Kuldeep Chand Kanwar (2026) [4] treats a complaint filed within the 15 days as no complaint at all, which cannot be cured by the lapse of time before cognizance. The Patna High Court in Subodh Kumar Rai (2026) [5] holds that a second notice cannot revive or extend limitation, and that the complainant must show sufficient cause under the proviso to Section 142(1)(b).

APPLICATION: The sources contain no dates other than the dishonour date of 11 November 2025. By way of illustration only, if the bank's information reached the payee on 11 November 2025, the notice had to be issued by about 11 December 2025. If notice were received on, say, 15 December 2025, the drawer's period would end on 30 December 2025. The complaint could then be filed only from 31 December 2025 and within one month after that. These dates are hypothetical, not facts from the record. The outer boundary is therefore not fixed by the dishonour date. It depends on the date of receipt of notice, which must be proved by postal or courier records.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT AND RISKS: The drawer's best arguments are that (i) the complaint was premature, filed before the 15 days ended [4][7]; (ii) it was filed over a month after the cause of action arose without a condonation application showing sufficient cause [5]; (iii) the notice was out of time under proviso (b); or (iv) the cheque was presented beyond the validity period. A complainant who relies on a second notice faces the Patna ruling [5]. The Himachal ruling [4] shows the drawer may take the prematurity point even at a late stage. In reply, the complainant should file a condonation application with the complaint if there is any doubt about delay. The sources do not decide what counts as sufficient cause, and the Supreme Court authority cited in the Patna decision (Japani Sahoo) is not among the sources.

PRACTICAL ADVICE: Obtain the bank return memo, the notice and the proof of delivery, and fix each date. Draft the complaint with the synopsis and affidavit of service directed in Sanjabij Tari [3], and file in the court with territorial jurisdiction under Section 142(2) [2].

relevant_law.summary: The offence is complete only if (a) the cheque was presented within six months of its date or within its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee gives written demand notice within thirty days of receiving information of return from the bank; and (c) the drawer fails to pay within fifteen days of receiving the notice. The provision [1] is the source of the cause of action. Clause (c) fixes the date from which the limitation period begins to run.

Section 142 [2] bars cognizance except on a written complaint by the payee or holder in due course. The complaint must be made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to Section 138. The court may take cognizance after that period if the complainant shows sufficient cause for the delay. Trial lies before a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class.

Territorial jurisdiction lies where the payee's collecting bank branch is situated if the cheque is delivered for collection through an account, or where the drawee bank branch is situated if the cheque is presented otherwise. This affects where the complaint must be filed within the limitation period [2].

The IPC definition in s. 416 [6] is the template: pretending to be another person, knowingly substituting one person for another, or representing oneself or another to be someone else, whether the person personated is real or imaginary. The punishment in s. 419 [2] is up to three years, or fine, or both. The corresponding BNS provision is s. 319 (with s. 319(2) for punishment). If the personation induced the complainant to hand over money or property, the heavier offence of cheating with dishonest inducement (IPC s. 420, BNS s. 318(4)) is added. Plain cheating (IPC s. 417 [1], BNS s. 318(2)) carries up to one year. Where a computer resource or communication device was used, the IT Act ss. 66C and 66D are commonly invoked in addition; I note them from the reference notes, not from the sources.

COURT POSITION: The Kerala High Court in Sanjeevan [4] holds that the offence needs a person cheated, the cheating effected by the s. 416 methods, and the victim acting on the false representation; absent reliance, the s. 419 charge failed. The Patna High Court in Prashant Katyayan [5] shows s. 419 being sustained on substitution while s. 420 was discarded because no delivery of property was alleged. The Bombay High Court in Kamat [3] reinforces that deception must be shown. These are persuasive only in Assam. None of the authorities is on online fraud, and no Supreme Court judgment is in the sources.

Electronic reporting is possible through the national cybercrime reporting portal and cyber police stations. Jurisdiction for inquiry and trial under the BNSS (as under the CrPC) can lie where any part of the offence occurred or where its consequences ensued, which would ordinarily include where the deceived person acted or suffered loss. ISSUE: The advocate asks which provisions protect the identity of a 10-year-old girl complainant and what police and media must do. Note first that the name '[NAME REDACTED]' appears in the query; it should not be used in any filing, order, cause list or draft, and the victim should be referred to by a pseudonym or initials.

LAW: The core protection sits in POCSO. Section 23 governs the media: no report may disclose the child's name, address, photograph, family, school, neighbourhood or any particulars that may identify her, and no report may be unfavourable to her reputation or invade her privacy. The Special Court can permit disclosure only in writing and only where it is in the child's interest. Section 24 and 26 govern police recording of the statement (at home or a place of the child's choice, by a woman officer, in plain clothes, no night detention at the police station, no contact with the accused). Sections 33, 36 and 37 govern the court: in camera trial, protection from seeing the accused, and non-disclosure of identity during investigation and trial save by reasoned direction. Outside POCSO, BNS s. 72 (IPC s. 228A for offences before 1 July 2024) penalises publication of a victim's identity, and BNSS s. 366-367 (CrPC s. 327) provide for in-camera proceedings and restrict publication of proceedings. All section numbers and contents here are from general knowledge and are not in the sources; the advocate must check them against the bare Acts.

Media houses are bound by s. 23; breach is punishable, and the advocate can apply to the Special Court for a direction or complain to the police.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The defence or a media house may argue that disclosure is permitted in the child's interest by the Special Court, or by next of kin through a recognised welfare body. The sources do not decide whether publishing the name of a deceased or consenting victim is permissible, nor the position on judgments.

The Calcutta Division Bench dealt with a first appeal and still pointed the wife to 'the competent civil court having jurisdiction' for a fresh s. 25 application [6]. None of the sources states the rules of Meghalaya High Court or the Meghalaya Family Court on this, or its territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction, so the advocate must confirm them from the court's own rules and registry.

APPLICABLE LAW: Section 25(1) gives either spouse the right to apply at the time of any decree or at any time afterwards, and the court may order a gross sum or periodical payment, even secured by a charge on immovable property [1]. Section 25(2) allows variation on changed circumstances; Kalyan Dey Chowdhury [5] stresses that a change must be shown.

COURT POSITION AND APPLICATION: Draft a written application, supported by an affidavit of assets and income of the applicant, together with an affidavit from the respondent. The Calcutta Division Bench calls this 'well-settled' practice [6]. Plead the respondent's income and property, the applicant's income and property, conduct and other circumstances, which are the factors listed in s. 25(1) [1]. Pray for a specific monthly or gross sum, and for a charge on identified immovable property if security is wanted. Attach salary slips, bank statements and property documents. Kalyan Dey Chowdhury [5] says the sum must befit the parties' status and the payer's capacity; the 25% net salary figure there was a fact-specific benchmark, not a rule. Sandhyarani [3] adds that the amount should allow dignity and not penury, and that a husband cannot dodge liability by giving up a job.

If the decree is already passed and the application was not made, Saranjit Kaur [6] confirms the application can still be filed afterwards. If you represent the husband, a late application does not by itself defeat the claim on that authority.

RISKS AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The opposing side can argue that Sandhyarani's rule of granting alimony without a prayer [3] is no longer needed, and that, per Saranjit Kaur [6], an application without materials fails. Where the marriage is void under s. 11 or the decree is of nullity, Mangala Lad [4] notes the view that s. 25 still applies, but the extract is mixed with other courts' reasoning, so verify before relying on it. The conduct of the parties is a statutory factor [1]. Section 25(3) [2] allows rescission on remarriage or unchastity. None of the sources decides limitation, court fee, or interim maintenance under s. 24 (not in the sources).

PRACTICAL ADVICE: File in the court that passed or is hearing the decree, and obtain the Meghalaya filing format from the registry.

relevant_law.summary: Any court exercising jurisdiction under the Act may, at the time of passing any decree or at any time subsequent thereto, on the application of either wife or husband, order the respondent to pay a gross sum or monthly/periodical sum not exceeding the applicant's life. The court weighs the respondent's income and property, the applicant's income and property, the conduct of the parties and other circumstances. The payment may be secured by a charge on the respondent's immovable property [1].

Under s. 25(2), the court may vary, modify or rescind its order if the circumstances of either party change. Under s. 25(3) (as reproduced in Rupali Mahanty (2022) [2]), the order may be varied or rescinded if the recipient has remarried, or the wife has not remained chaste, or the husband has had sexual intercourse outside wedlock. Section 25(3) is not in the extract of s. 25 at [1]; confirm its current text from the Act.

review_notes: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 s.25: commencement and repeal dates are not recorded for this provision, so whether it was in force on the relevant date has NOT been verified; check the Act's commencement and any amending or repealing instrument before relying on it.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: Allahabad [1][3][5], Gujarat [2] and Gauhati [4] all treat entrustment and dishonest misappropriation or breach of the mode of discharge as the core of the offence. Four of the five decisions quash or reject proceedings where entrustment or dishonesty is not pleaded.
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: Shikha Bishnoi [5] declined to interfere under s.482 CrPC where entrustment was admitted and left the defence to trial. Kuldeep Singh [1], Surendra Singh [3] and Bhatnagar [2] quashed on the face of the allegations. The difference is factual: admitted entrustment versus none alleged. No source is from the Punjab and Haryana High Court, so no conflict with that court can be assessed.
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: The sources show courts scrutinising FIRs and complaints to separate civil disputes from criminal breach of trust. They do not address how the BNS enhancement of the maximum to five years has been treated, and no post-2024 BNS s.316 decision is supplied.

answer.conclusion:
The sources do not contain any Punjab and Haryana High Court decision from 2018, so I cannot report how that court interpreted IPC s.406. What they do show is a consistent High Court approach: the accused is liable only where entrustment and dishonest misappropriation are shown. For a 2018 offence, plead IPC ss.405/406 with BNS s.316 as the corresponding provision, noting the maximum rose from three to five years. Before relying on any Punjab and Haryana authority, obtain the certified copy of the judgment or check the court's website. Also verify Onkar Nath Mishra against the official Supreme Court report, because it is only quoted here.



📋 **Law Transition Note (1 July 2024):**
The IPC 1860 → BNS 2023, CrPC 1973 → BNSS 2023, and IEA 1872 → BSA 2023.
• The **penal** code follows the date of the **offence**: the IPC for an offence committed before 1 July 2024 (s.358 BNS), the BNS on or after it.
• **Procedure and evidence** follow the date the **proceeding was begun**: the CrPC and the IEA continue only for a proceeding already pending on 1 July 2024 (s.531(2)(a) BNSS, s.170(2) BSA); an FIR or case begun on or after that date follows the BNSS and the BSA, even for an earlier offence.
answer.issue: How did the Punjab and Haryana High Court interpret IPC s.406 (criminal breach of trust) in 2018, and how does that map onto BNS s.316? The sources supplied contain no Punjab and Haryana High Court judgment, so that part cannot be answered from them.

precedents.case_name: Kuldeep Singh @ Kala v State of U.P. (CRLP/32510/2018)
precedents.holding_summary: Sets out the ingredients of s.405 IPC: entrustment, then dishonest misappropriation, conversion, use or disposal in violation of law or contract. The complaint's allegations did not satisfy ss.406/420 IPC, so the FIR and subsequent proceedings were quashed [1].

precedents.case_name: S.N. Bhatnagar v State of Gujarat (CR.MA/12430/2005)
precedents.holding_summary: Failure to recover loans and advances is not misappropriation absent allegations that the funds travelled back to the accused. It may be a breach of Companies Act duties but not an IPC offence. On cheating, dishonest intention must exist at inception, and mere breach of contract is not an offence [2].

precedents.case_name: Surendra Singh v State of U.P. (A482/4775/2020)
precedents.holding_summary: Relying on Onkar Nath Mishra v State (NCT of Delhi), the court set aside a summoning order because there was no entrustment. Two parts are required: an obligation over property, then dishonest dealing contrary to it [3]. Onkar Nath Mishra is quoted only through this judgment and was not itself supplied.

precedents.case_name: Abhijit Saikia v State of Assam (Crl.Pet./32/2024)
precedents.holding_summary: Lists the essentials of s.405 as entrustment, then dishonest use or disposal in violation of law or contract. The court found no s.406 case on the FIR and case diary, but dismissed the petition because a prima facie case under ss.420/468 was made out [4].

precedents.case_name: Shikha Bishnoi v State of U.P. (A482/14054/2020)
precedents.holding_summary: Offence is complete when the trust is infringed. Where the money was deferred on demand, breach occurred only at the last denial, so the s.468 CrPC limitation bar did not apply. Where entrustment was admitted, the accused's defence is for trial and not for s.482 CrPC. The report does not identify a majority opinion, so these passages are attributable only to that text, not to a settled holding [5].

answer.reasoned_analysis:
ISSUE: You asked how the Punjab and Haryana High Court read IPC s.406 in 2018. None of the five sources comes from that court, so I cannot state its 2018 position. Any Punjab and Haryana authority you cite must be taken from its certified copy or the court's own website. I have not guessed at case names.

LAW: BNS s.316(1) reproduces the IPC s.405 definition, including the two Explanations on PF and ESI contributions. Section 316(2) replaces IPC s.406, raising the maximum from three to five years (the three-year figure appears in [1] and [5]). Because the offence date decides the code, a 2018 transaction is charged under IPC ss.405/406. Under BNS s.358 the old provisions are saved. Procedure follows the date proceedings began: an FIR lodged on or after 1 July 2024 follows the BNSS even for a 2018 offence.

COURT POSITION FROM THE SOURCES: The Allahabad High Court in Kuldeep Singh [1] breaks s.405 into entrustment plus dishonest misappropriation or violation of law or contract, and quashed the FIR when the complaint disclosed neither. Surendra Singh [3], quoting Onkar Nath Mishra, describes two parts: creation of an obligation over property, then dishonest dealing contrary to it. There, absence of entrustment was fatal to the summoning order. The Gujarat High Court in Bhatnagar [2] held that failing to recover advances is not misappropriation without a trace of the funds back to the accused. [AUTHORITY NOT CONFIRMED — no retrieved passage could be identified as the majority opinion of the Bench] The Gauhati High Court in Abhijit Saikia [4] applied the same two-limb test.

APPLICATION: For an accused, the strongest argument is that the complaint pleads no entrustment, or only a debt, advance or contractual payment, and no dishonest intent. Cite [1], [3] and [2]. Add that where cheating is also alleged, dishonest intention must exist at inception [2].

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: The complainant will rely on Shikha Bishnoi [5]. Where entrustment is admitted, whether the accused dishonestly breached the trust is a matter of evidence, and the High Court should not weigh evidence in a s.482 CrPC (BNSS s.528) petition. Its report records no identified majority opinion, so it is weak authority. Abhijit Saikia [4] also shows that quashing one count does not end the case if cheating is made out.

LIMITS: All five are High Court decisions, so none binds the Punjab and Haryana High Court. The Supreme Court decision Onkar Nath Mishra reaches us only as quoted in [3], and the Gujarat reference to All Cargo Movers (India) Private Limited v Dhanesh Badarmal Jain likewise appears only through [2]. Neither was independently supplied.

relevant_law.summary: Defines criminal breach of trust: a person entrusted with property or dominion over it dishonestly misappropriates or converts it, or dishonestly uses or disposes of it in violation of a direction of law or a legal contract, or wilfully suffers another to do so. Explanations 1 and 2 deem employer-deducted PF and ESI contributions to be entrusted property.
Basic punishment: imprisonment up to five years, or fine, or both. Under IPC s.406 the maximum was three years, as the Allahabad decisions [1][5] note. The BNS therefore enhances the penalty.

Aggravated forms: carrier, wharfinger or warehouse-keeper (up to 7 years); clerk or servant (up to 7 years); public servant, banker, merchant, factor, broker, attorney or agent (life, or up to 10 years, and fine).

An offence committed before 1 July 2024 is charged under the IPC. An offence committed on or after that date is charged under the BNS. A 2018 transaction is therefore tried under IPC ss.405/406, with BNS s.316 as the corresponding provision.

comparative_analysis.agreements_between_courts: उपलब्ध स्रोतों में कोई ऐसा निर्णय नहीं है जो IPC 324/BNS 118 से जुड़े आवेदन की प्रक्रिया या पंजाब एवं हरियाणा उच्च न्यायालय की प्रक्रिया तय करता हो। State of Haryana v. S.K. Singhal (1999) [3], Sandeep Gupta v. Union of India (2025) [2] और Secretary to the Govt. of Haryana v. Vidya Sagar (2009) [4] सेवा-विधि से संबंधित हैं (स्वैच्छिक सेवानिवृत्ति और चिकित्सा प्रतिपूर्ति), और Bhagwan Dei v. JVVNL (2023) [5] राजस्थान उच्च न्यायालय का अपील वापसी का आदेश है; इनका प्रस्तुत प्रश्न से कोई संबंध नहीं है।
comparative_analysis.conflicts_or_differences: स्रोतों में इस विषय पर कोई परस्पर विरोधी मत नहीं है, क्योंकि कोई स्रोत इस विषय को छूता ही नहीं।
comparative_analysis.trend_analysis: स्रोतों से इस विषय पर विधि के विकास का कोई निष्कर्ष नहीं निकलता। केवल इतना स्पष्ट है कि IPC 324 के स्थान पर BNS 118 आई है और प्रक्रिया की संहिता भी CrPC से BNSS हो गई है।

answer.conclusion:
धारा 324 [1] से अपने-आप उच्च न्यायालय में आवेदन का कोई अधिकार नहीं बनता; आवेदन की प्रक्रिया दंड प्रक्रिया संहिता से निकलेगी, और उसका स्वरूप (अग्रिम या नियमित जमानत, कार्यवाही रद्द करना, पुनरीक्षण) आपके मुवक्किल की स्थिति पर निर्भर है। सबसे पहले अपराध की तिथि देखें: 1 जुलाई 2024 से पहले का हो तो IPC 324, बाद का हो तो BNS 118(1)। फिर FIR की तिथि देखें: 1 जुलाई 2024 या उसके बाद की FIR पर BNSS की धाराएँ (482, 483, 528) लागू होंगी। उपलब्ध स्रोतों में कोई ऐसा निर्णय नहीं है जो इस विषय को तय करे, इसलिए इस पर भरोसा करने योग्य कोई उदाहरण यहाँ नहीं दिया जा सकता। कृपया तथ्य (अपराध और FIR की तिथि, आवेदन का उद्देश्य) बताएँ, तथा BNSS की धाराओं का पाठ और पंजाब एवं हरियाणा उच्च न्यायालय की फाइलिंग प्रक्रिया आधिकारिक राजपत्र और न्यायालय की वेबसाइट से सत्यापित करें।

⚠️ CITATION CONFIDENCE: 2 of 3 provisions read from their own text; 1 not found in the sources. Independently verify all cited cases before court use.

The INDIAN-PENAL-CODE-1860 s.324: उद्धृत रूप में यह प्रावधान इस प्रश्न को नियंत्रित करने वाली तिथि पर लागू था या नहीं, इसका सत्यापन नहीं हुआ है; भरोसा करने से पहले प्रारंभ, संशोधन और निरसन की अधिसूचनाओं से इसकी जाँच करें।
answer.issue: भारतीय दंड संहिता की धारा 324 (खतरनाक हथियारों या साधनों से स्वेच्छया चोट पहुँचाना) से उत्पन्न मामले में पंजाब और हरियाणा उच्च न्यायालय में आवेदन किस प्रावधान और किस प्रक्रिया से दायर किया जाए। प्रश्न में आवेदन का प्रकार (अग्रिम जमानत, नियमित जमानत, FIR/कार्यवाही रद्द करना, राजीनामा आदि) और अपराध की तिथि नहीं बताई गई है।
answer.law_staleness_warning: ⚠️ Superseded provisions cited: IPC s.324 -> BNS s.118. | Which code applies depends on dates: The penal code follows the date the offence was committed: an offence committed before 1 July 2024 is charged and punished under the Indian Penal Code, which section 358 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita saves, and one committed on or after that date under the BNS. One continuing offence that runs across 1 July 2024 is charged once, never split by date into an IPC charge and a BNS charge (section 9(1) of the BNS allows one punishment for an offence made up of parts), and under the BNS, since it was still being committed after that date (section 1(3) of the BNS); separate offences are each charged under the code in force when each was committed. The procedure follows the date the proceeding was begun: only an appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation already pending immediately before 1 July 2024 continues under the Code of Criminal Procedure (section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita), and the evidence in it under the Indian Evidence Act (section 170 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam); a proceeding begun on or after that date, including an FIR lodged then for an offence committed before it, follows the BNSS and the BSA. Cite the repealed equivalent in brackets where it helps the court.
answer.reasoned_analysis: मुद्दा: प्रश्न है कि IPC की धारा 324 के अंतर्गत आरोप होने पर पंजाब और हरियाणा उच्च न्यायालय में आवेदन 'कैसे' दायर किया जाए। प्रश्न में आवेदन का स्वरूप स्पष्ट नहीं है, और यही उत्तर की पहली शर्त है। धारा 324 [1] स्वयं कोई आवेदन-प्रक्रिया नहीं बताती; यह केवल अपराध का स्वरूप और दंड (तीन वर्ष तक कारावास या जुर्माना या दोनों) तय करती है। अतः आवेदन की प्रक्रिया दंड प्रक्रिया संहिता के प्रावधानों से निकलेगी। लागू संहिता का निर्धारण: दंड संहिता अपराध की तिथि से तय होगी। 1 जुलाई 2024 से पहले का अपराध IPC 324 [1] के अंतर्गत आएगा, और उसके बाद का अपराध BNS 118(1) के अंतर्गत, जिसमें दंड तीन वर्ष तक कारावास या बीस हजार रुपये तक जुर्माना या दोनों है। यदि अपराध लगातार चलने वाला हो और 1 जुलाई 2024 के पार जाता हो, तो BNS लागू होगी। प्रक्रिया की संहिता कार्यवाही प्रारंभ होने की तिथि से तय होगी: केवल वही अन्वेषण, जाँच, विचारण, अपील या आवेदन, जो 1 जुलाई 2024 से ठीक पहले लंबित था, CrPC से चलेगा (BNSS 531(2)(a)); 1 जुलाई 2024 या उसके बाद दर्ज FIR, चाहे अपराध पहले का हो, BNSS से चलेगी। उदाहरणार्थ, पुराने अपराध पर नई FIR में आरोप IPC 324 का होगा, पर अग्रिम जमानत का आवेदन BNSS 482 (CrPC 438) के अंतर्गत होगा। संभावित आवेदन: (क) अग्रिम जमानत - BNSS 482 / CrPC 438; (ख) नियमित जमानत - BNSS 483 / CrPC 439; (ग) FIR या कार्यवाही रद्द करना, जिसमें पक्षकारों के बीच समझौता भी आता है - BNSS 528 / CrPC 482; (घ) पुनरीक्षण - BNSS 438 / CrPC 397। इनमें से केवल पहली तीन धाराओं (482, 483 और 528) का नाम इस उत्तर के संदर्भ में दिया गया है, और उनका पाठ उपलब्ध सामग्री में नहीं है; इसलिए उनकी शर्तें, सीमाएँ और अंतर्वस्तु प्रमाणित प्रति या आधिकारिक विधि-ग्रंथ से देखनी होंगी। न्यायिक स्थिति: उपलब्ध स्रोतों में कोई निर्णय इस प्रश्न पर नहीं है। State of Haryana v. S.K. Singhal (1999) [3], Sandeep Gupta (2025) [2] और Vidya Sagar (2009) [4] सेवा-विधि के निर्णय हैं तथा [5] एक अपील वापसी का आदेश है; इन पर भरोसा करना भ्रामक होगा। प्रतिपक्ष का सबसे मजबूत तर्क: राज्य यह कह सकता है कि यदि आवेदन अग्रिम जमानत का है, तो अभियुक्त पहले सत्र न्यायालय जाए, या समझौते के आधार पर कार्यवाही रद्द करने का आवेदन समय-पूर्व है। इन दोनों आपत्तियों पर क्या स्थिति है, यह भी स्रोतों से तय नहीं होता। जोखिम: गलत संहिता का उल्लेख (CrPC की जगह BNSS या उलटा) और आवेदन के स्वरूप का गलत चयन। व्यावहारिक सुझाव: सबसे पहले अपराध की तिथि और FIR की तिथि तय करें; फिर आवेदन का स्वरूप चुनें; तब पंजाब और हरियाणा उच्च न्यायालय की अद्यतन रजिस्ट्री-प्रक्रिया, फाइलिंग नियम और प्रारूप उच्च न्यायालय की आधिकारिक वेबसाइट या रजिस्ट्री से सत्यापित करें, क्योंकि वह जानकारी इन स्रोतों में नहीं है।

relevant_law.summary: शूटिंग, छेदने या काटने के किसी उपकरण, आग, गर्म पदार्थ, विष, संक्षारक या विस्फोटक पदार्थ अथवा किसी पशु के साधन से स्वेच्छया चोट पहुँचाने पर तीन वर्ष तक के कारावास, या जुर्माने, या दोनों का दंड है। यह धारा 334 (प्रकोपन पर चोट) के मामलों पर लागू नहीं होती। यह धारा केवल अपराध और दंड तय करती है; उच्च न्यायालय में आवेदन की प्रक्रिया इसमें नहीं है।

BNS 118(1) में वही साधन गिनाए गए हैं, दंड तीन वर्ष तक कारावास या बीस हजार रुपये तक जुर्माना या दोनों है। BNS 118(2) में खतरनाक साधनों से घोर उपहति पर आजीवन कारावास, या एक से दस वर्ष का कारावास और जुर्माना है। 1 जुलाई 2024 या उसके बाद किए गए अपराध पर BNS लागू होगी; उससे पहले के अपराध पर IPC 324 (BNS 358 से संरक्षित)।

इन धाराओं के अंतर्गत क्रमशः अग्रिम जमानत, नियमित जमानत और उच्च न्यायालय की अंतर्निहित शक्ति के आवेदन आते हैं। यहाँ इनका पाठ उपलब्ध सामग्री में नहीं दिया गया है, अतः उनकी अंतर्वस्तु स्मृति से नहीं बताई जा रही। कौन-सा आवेदन चलेगा, यह इस पर निर्भर है कि कार्यवाही 1 जुलाई 2024 से पहले या बाद में प्रारंभ हुई (BNSS 531(2)(a))।
